headline: The Volume Is Melting Away
lede: SPY is up, the RSI is pushing into overbought territory, and the shares changing hands each day are falling toward levels not seen outside of holiday half-sessions. Michael Kramer of Mott Capital Management distilled it in five words. The question his chart raises is whether thinning volume is a warning, a structural artifact, or simply the quiet that tends to follow a storm.
body:
Markets have a long memory for the relationship between price and volume. The old technician's rule — that a rally should be confirmed by rising volume and that a rally on falling volume is to be distrusted — dates at least to Richard Wyckoff's work in the early twentieth century, and it has survived because it encodes something real: when prices rise and fewer participants are willing to transact, it suggests that conviction is waning even as the headline number climbs. What Michael Kramer, founder of Mott Capital Management and the voice behind the @MichaelMOTTCM account, flagged in a five-word post on X was exactly this dissonance. A TradingView chart co-authored with user Jay1104 showed SPY — the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, the world's most liquid equity security — printing a single session at just 22.81 million shares. Against a 30-day average daily volume of roughly 68.85 million shares as of early May 2026, that reading is barely a third of normal.

The broader context matters enormously. SPY's first quarter of 2026 was anything but quiet: the index fell sharply on successive waves of tariff escalation, and average daily volume on the heaviest distribution days — the sessions in which price fell on outsized turnover — ran at 86 to 115 million shares. That is the signature of genuine institutional selling: effort matching result, in Wyckoff's phrase. The subsequent recovery, which carried SPY from its Q1 lows back toward $715 with the RSI (Relative Strength Index — a momentum oscillator that compares average gains to average losses over fourteen days; readings above 70 conventionally signal an overbought condition) touching 70.65, happened on dramatically reduced volume. The effort did not match the result, which is the classic profile of what technicians call a **distribution day** pattern in reverse: price rising without the buying pressure normally required to sustain it.

Two competing explanations deserve equal weight. The bearish reading is the traditional one: falling volume on a rally signals that the smart money is not adding exposure, that the move is being driven by short-covering or forced buying — retirement-account contributions, index-rebalancing flows, options-market mechanics — rather than fresh long conviction. The April 2026 recovery in SPY was, in material part, a product of **vanna flows**: when implied volatility collapsed after a period of acute stress, dealers who had sold put options were able to reduce their hedging short positions in SPY, mechanically lifting the index without any fundamental buyer entering the market. Prior to that reversal, since approximately April 20, net buy volume had already been declining even as price held its uptrend — a divergence that volume analysts note tends to precede price itself turning lower.

The bullish, or at least agnostic, counter-argument is structural. The options market has undergone a transformation so rapid that it likely distorts every comparison of spot-equity volume to historical baselines. Zero-days-to-expiration contracts — **0DTE options** (calls and puts that expire within the same trading session, used for precise intraday hedging and speculation) — accounted for 59% of all SPX index option volume by early 2026 and approximately 45% of all SPY option volume on a typical day. When a trader can express a directional view on the S&P 500 by purchasing a same-day option rather than buying or selling shares directly, the natural gravitational pull of that activity toward the options market reduces spot-equity volume mechanically, independently of any change in conviction. This structural migration has been ongoing since the CBOE introduced full daily expirations in 2022; every comparison of 2026 SPY volume to the 2018 or 2019 baseline carries a hidden denominator problem.

A third explanation, neither bullish nor bearish, is simply seasonal. Markets in the post-earnings-season window — roughly the stretch from mid-April through Memorial Day — routinely experience lower participation as institutional desks close their books on the quarter, hedge funds reduce gross exposure pending summer positioning decisions, and the sell-side's research calendar enters a quieter phase. The aphorism "sell in May and go away" is imprecise as a trading rule, but it captures a genuine empirical regularity: realized volatility and average daily volume both tend to compress in this window. Thin markets are not necessarily fragile markets, but they are more susceptible to sharp moves on any surprise, because the bid-ask depth that absorbs large orders in high-volume environments simply is not there.

Kramer's chart adds one more data point that complicates a clean reading: the RSI is elevated, the price is near the high end of its recovery range, and the volume is not there to support either a convincing breakout or a convincing distribution. That ambiguity is, perhaps, the most honest summary of where the index sits. The weight of the tape — the sum of historical precedents, structural shifts, and seasonal patterns — does not resolve neatly into a buy or a sell signal. It resolves into what Kramer's post implicitly communicated: attentiveness. Volume is the market's way of reporting its own confidence. When it melts away at the top, that report deserves to be read carefully, even if the reading remains inconclusive.

concepts.definition: The total number of shares (or contracts) that change hands in a given security during a defined period. Volume is treated as a proxy for market conviction: high volume validates price moves; low volume on a directional move raises questions about the move's sustainability.

A session in which a major index closes lower on volume higher than the previous day's, interpreted as evidence that large institutional investors are selling — 'distributing' — their holdings into the market rather than accumulating.

A momentum oscillator, developed by J. Welles Wilder Jr. in 1978, that compares the average magnitude of recent gains to recent losses over a lookback period (typically 14 days) and scales the result to a 0–100 range. Readings above 70 conventionally indicate overbought conditions; readings below 30 indicate oversold.

Dealer hedging adjustments triggered by changes in implied volatility. Vanna measures how much a dealer's delta (directional equity exposure) shifts when volatility moves; when IV falls sharply, dealers who sold puts reduce their short equity hedges, mechanically lifting share prices — a 'vol crush rally' — independent of any fundamental buyer.

Zero-days-to-expiration options — calls or puts that expire on the same trading day they are purchased. Their explosive growth since the CBOE introduced daily S&P 500 expirations in 2022 has structurally migrated intraday speculation away from the spot equity market into the options complex, compressing measured share volume even when overall market activity is robust.

A technical analysis framework developed by Richard Wyckoff in the early twentieth century, centered on reading price-and-volume relationships to infer the intentions of large ('composite') market operators. Its core principle — that effort (volume) should confirm result (price movement) — underpins most modern volume-based analysis.

fact_check: SPY closing price ~$715 and RSI(14) of 70.65 per OCR of the TradingView chart in the post. Session volume of 22.81M shares per chart OCR. SPY 30-day ADV of ~68.85M as of May 4, 2026 per YCharts. 0DTE share of SPY options volume (~45%) per SpotGamma; 59% share of SPX volume per CBOE/CME Group data. Q1 2026 distribution-day volume spikes (86–115M) sourced from Anna Coulling / modigin.com analysis. Michael Kramer confirmed as founder of Mott Capital Management; SEC registration verified at adviserinfo.sec.gov. He is NOT Michael Kantrowitz of Piper Sandler — different individuals.
thread_summary: Single post by @MichaelMOTTCM (Michael J. Kramer, Mott Capital Management) accompanied by a TradingView daily candlestick chart for SPY (co-authored with Jay1104), showing SPY at $715.12 (+0.17%), session volume of 22.81M shares, and RSI(14) at 70.65. The five-word caption — 'The volume is just melting away.' — flags a price-volume divergence: the index recovered to overbought RSI levels on dramatically thin participation relative to the prior months' elevated volatility-driven turnover.
